items.title: US home price insights — November 2026
items.description: Overview: Home prices continue to rise nationally, up 1.7%, but momentum is moderating with a 0.3% monthly decline, and annual growth forecasted to slow to 0.9%. Compared with August, appreciation strengthened in about half of metros and weakened in the other half, suggesting no single national trajectory. Annual appreciation was led by northeastern and Great Lakes states, paced by Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). National home price growth September 2026 data Source: Cotality ‍ Affordability meter Source: Cotality ‍ ‍ Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract retiring population and offer affordable homes. Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality Chief Economist Insights from Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp As autumn arrived, the U.S. housing market cooled further. In September 2026, single-family home prices rose just 1.7% year-over-year and dropped 0.3% from August, pushing the national median above $400,000. This was the largest monthly decline since 2022 and the third consecutive September without growth, as high mortgage rates curbed summer demand. Normally, home prices edge up about 0.2% in September. But national averages still hide a key divide: Every Northeast and Midwest state saw annual price gains, while four Western and two Southern states posted declines. The market is nearly evenly split between areas accelerating and those slowing. Many Northeastern and Midwestern markets have gained 25% to 30% since mid-2022, while much of the West and Texas have seen little or no net growth. This regional divide sharpened considerably heading into the final stretch of the year. Chronic inventory shortages in the Great Lakes and New England fueled strong annual gains— Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). Meanwhile, prices dropped in former boom states: Washington (-1.0%), Wyoming (-0.7%), Texas (-0.4%), Hawaii (-0.1%), and Utah (-0.0%). Since June 2022, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New Jersey have surged 30–31%, while Washington, Colorado, and Texas are up less than 1%, and D.C. is down 2%. “Potential homebuyers are feeling the pinch from rising costs across the board, especially for daily living expenses,” said Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp. “Meanwhile, limited job opportunities and slow wage growth are making households reluctant to move.” Leading metros for recent price growth include Cleveland, Albany, Providence, Greensboro, and St. Louis—places marked by affordability, job growth, in-migration, and recent price resets. In contrast, the fastest-cooling markets, like Augusta, Austin, Seattle, San Jose, and Washington, DC, have seen job losses, higher inventory, and declining affordability. Rising mortgage rates have sharply reduced affordability. When the 30-year fixed rate rose from 6.5% to 7.5%, the monthly payment on a median-priced home jumped $300, pushing the required annual income to $103,000. In California, buyers need $180,900 for a $754,500 median home. In Florida and Texas ($369,750 median), higher insurance and taxes often push total costs above borrowing limits, fueling declines in metros like Austin (-2.0%) and Dallas (-1.0%). “Elevated mortgage rates are expected to limit home buying opportunities in 2027,” concluded Dr. Hepp. “However, more inventory and greater buyer bargaining power will keep home price growth subdued, improving affordability. Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract retiring population and offer affordable homes.” -Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality’s Chief Economist Dive deeper Home price indexes Top 10 hottest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Top 10 coolest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Which areas are affordable? items.title: The math behind staying put: When does buying a home beat renting?
items.description: The math behind staying put: When does buying a home beat renting? by Arben Skivjani Posted November 2, 2026 in Rent Growth Rate In January 2021, mortgage rates hit a record low of 2.65%. On October 29, 2026, Freddie Mac’s 30-year rate was 7.24%, more than a full point higher than a year ago. Including property taxes and insurance, the monthly cost of owning the typical home now runs about $930 more than the rent on an average apartment. A difference that size drives a lot of decisions in the apartment market, starting with whether renters keep renting or buy a home. So how far would rates have to fall for the two to even out? Farther than most people think. To see how we got here, I went back to four moments when the math looked very different, from the high rates of 2000 to the record lows of 2021, and followed a household earning the median income through each one. At each moment, I compared the monthly loan payment on a typical home, using a 30-year fixed mortgage with 20% down, with the rent on an average apartment. On that basis alone, today’s payment of about $2,300 runs nearly $380 above the $1,915 average rent in our data. Taxes and insurance make up the rest, and I’ll get to those. Through all four moments, renters have been responding to the math. In our data, they’re renewing more often than they did 20 years ago, and today they’re signing the longest renewal leases since our records began in 2002. 2000 and 2006: A much smaller gap In the spring of 2000, the 30-year rate was about 8.3%, the kind of number that would stop most buyers today. But homes were cheaper relative to incomes. The median single-family home sold for about $144,000, according to the National Association of Realtors, or about 3.4 times the median household income. The monthly payment came to about $870, only about $40 more than the average rent in our data, and took about 25% of the Census Bureau’s median household income. Six years later, near the peak of the housing boom, the math had shifted. Rates had eased, but the median price had climbed to $220,000. The payment now ran about $160 above average rent. The difference had grown, but for many households it was still manageable. The down payment had grown, too, from more than two-thirds of a year’s median income in 2000 to more than 90% by 2006. Meanwhile, apartment occupancy slipped from 96% to just under 95%, after years of easy credit had pulled many renters into homeownership. 2012: Owning costs less than renting After the housing crash, the picture flipped. By the end of 2012, the median home had fallen to about $181,000, and the 30-year rate had dropped to about 3.4%. The monthly payment was about $410 less than average rent and took only 15% of median income, the lowest share of the five moments. On paper, owning was clearly the cheaper choice. In practice, it wasn’t that simple. Lenders had tightened their standards after the crisis, and saving a 20% down payment was still a big hurdle. Residents were already renewing more often, 49% at the end of 2012, up from 46% in 2006. For a lot of households, the math on paper and the reality didn’t line up. 2021: The cheapest money on record Then came the pandemic, and with it record-low mortgage rates. Home prices were climbing fast, with the median at about $335,000 in early 2021, but with rates under 3%, the monthly payment was still more than $300 below average rent. At 19% of median income, the payment was easy to manage for a typical household. It was a strong time for apartments, too. Job growth came back quickly, and apartment demand surged. By early 2022, occupancy in our data had climbed to 97.5%, the highest going back to 2000. Cheap mortgages and a strong rental market existed side by side, because the economy was creating new households fast enough to fill both. That window didn’t stay open for long. As inflation picked up, the Fed began raising rates in 2022, and mortgage rates followed. By the end of that year, the 30-year rate was above 6%, and households that had waited to buy faced a very different payment on a similar home. Many decided to keep renting. 2026: The widest gap of the five Today, rates and prices are both pushing the cost of owning higher. The median home sells for about $420,000, roughly 25% more than in early 2021, and the mortgage rate is more than twice as high. That puts the monthly loan payment at about $2,300, roughly 20% above average rent. Even in 2006, near the peak of the boom, the payment ran only about 16% above rent. For a family earning the median household income, about $87,500 a year, that payment would take nearly a third of their income, up from 15% in 2012 and above the 30% line that lenders and housing economists often use as a sign of strain. The home itself costs about 4.8 times their annual income, the highest multiple of the five moments. Add property taxes and insurance, and owning looks even more expensive. Using a national average effective property tax rate of 0.9%, according to ATTOM, and an average homeowners insurance premium of about $2,900 a year, according to Insurance.com, the full monthly cost of owning the median home comes to about $2,840. That’s about $930 above average rent, before a single repair bill. Then there’s the down payment. Twenty percent down on today’s median home is about $84,000, nearly a full year of median household income and the highest share of the five moments. It’s no surprise that the typical first-time buyer is now 40 years old, according to the National Association of Realtors, and that first-time buyers made up just 21% of purchases, a record low. Renters are staying put Renters are doing the same math, and it shows. In Realpage data, 57% of renters whose leases were up in the third quarter of 2026 chose to renew, compared with 46% back in 2006. And when they renew, they’re signing on for longer. items.title: Construction Job Openings Rise in September
items.description: Construction Job Openings Rise in September November 3, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments The number of open positions in the construction sector increased in September per the Bureau of Labor Statistics Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) . The current level of open jobs is down from three years ago due to declines in construction activity, particularly in housing. Nonetheless, strength in construction in subsectors like data center construction is creating demand for construction workers. Further, increasing immigration enforcement actions are having an effect on worker availability, which is also contributing to upward pressure for the number of open positions. The number of open jobs for the overall economy increased in September, rising to 7.5 million. The September reading was higher than a year ago (7.17 million). The September data revealed a rise in job openings across many sectors of the U.S. economy as economic growth remains solid. The number of open construction sector jobs increased in September, rising from 262,000 in August to 298,000 in September. This total is higher than the total from a year ago (206,000). The chart below notes a declining trend for the construction job openings rate from 2023 to 2025 (after Fed tightening of monetary policy) followed by a recent rising trend for open positions in construction, albeit with significant month to month volatility. While home building employment has declined over the last year , other sectors of the construction industry have expanded (e.g. data center construction). The industry also faces challenges in terms of no-shows at work sites related to immigration enforcement. The construction job openings rate increased to 3.4% in September and is up from 2.4% a year ago. The construction hiring rate increased to 4.3% in September, up from the 4.1% rate estimated a year ago. The layoff rate in construction was 1.6% in September. The quits rate posted a notable rise in September, increasing to 2.4%. There were 198,000 total quits in that month, compared to 127,000 a year ago. items.title: Newrez adds ex-Rocket exec, highlighting industry tech pivot
items.description: Newrez adds ex-Rocket exec, highlighting industry tech pivot By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 03, 2026, 1:39 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "There is tremendous opportunity to build on that foundation and set a new standard in our industry for servicing excellence," — Newrez's Jay Jones. Forward Look: On the horizon: A scheduled transition to a new servicing platform starting in early 2027. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content Newrez added top servicing leader Jay Jones to its executive suite, marking another development in the mortgage industry's technology race, as recent appointments among the largest players demonstrate today's prioritization of artificial intelligence. Newrez Chief Servicing Officer Jay Jones The Fort Washington, Pennsylvania-based company named the former Rocket Mortgage leader chief servicing officer this week. Most recently, Jones held the same title at Rocket, the country's largest servicer. "Servicing is a foundation of our business, and bringing in someone of Jay's caliber speaks to the importance we place on our platform and servicing team," said Newrez President Baron Silverstein in a press release. Jones' appointment comes during a period of heightened consolidation within the home finance community , with leading mortgage researchers warning about the potential of a significant reduction in lending volume through 2027 . Although an ongoing wave of layoffs also looks likely to persist for several months, Newrez's move shows the pursuit of top-level tech-fluent executives continues among the largest companies despite industry downsizing. Jones previously served in senior management at Mr. Cooper, prior to its acquisition by Rocket in 2025, and played a pivotal role in integrating the servicing portfolios at the two mortgage giants. His career in mortgage servicing also includes tenures at Celink, OneWest Bank and IndyMac. Even while the outlook for originations gets bleaker, recent trends indicate some companies are willing to designate resources to build their servicing segments into business conduits , thanks to the recapture opportunities it offers. The mortgage industry's focus on tech and servicing strategy Upgraded servicing technology emerged as a primary focus of Newrez investment this year, even before a sudden surge in mortgage rates in second and third quarters destroyed prospects for a 2026 originations upturn. In February, its parent company, Rithm Capital, upped its investment into AI-backed servicing platform Valon Technologies, taking a minority ownership stake in the latter, while announcing plans to transfer its entire portfolio of loans onto the system. Company executives said during its recent earnings call that artificial intelligence investments across Newrez will drive $125 million in savings. Jones will lead transition efforts to the Valon platform beginning in early 2027, in addition to holding oversight of Newrez's $879 billion servicing portfolio. "Jay understands what our servicing clients and homeowners expect from us, and as we move to ValonOS, he will help build the next era of our industry-leading servicing experience," Silverstein said. In its most recent earnings, Rithm reported pre-tax income of almost $605 million at the mortgage unit. Servicing generated over $306 million in revenue to the bottom line. "Newrez has built a servicing business that clients trust and homeowners count on, pairing deep human expertise with strong digital capabilities. There is tremendous opportunity to build on that foundation and set a new standard in our industry for servicing excellence," Jones said. Tech expertise as a leadership prerequisite Newrez's announcement also shines a spotlight on the mortgage industry's propensity today to elevate technology experts to the highest positions, as companies look toward their futures when deciding to add or shuffle C-suite leadership. Prior to the blockbuster deal that joined Rocket and Mr. Cooper, Jones' former companies both were already making significant technology investments , even before the rapid growth of artificial intelligence. Two of the largest platforms used by lenders or servicers today, Dark Matter Technologies and Sagent, both opted to promote experienced software leaders Vikas Rao and Sridhar Sharma to CEOs of their respective companies in major leadership shakeups this year. Owners of the latter specifically cited the necessity of having technology expertise at the helm to lead it in the artificial intelligence age. items.title: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit
items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman. Both stocks have moved more than 60% higher since Oct. 14. Ackman believes both names can see a "10-fold" increase from current share prices. Bill Ackman, chief executive officer of Pershing Square Capital Management LP, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) over the last month. Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday. Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS. The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then. Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control. VIDEO 22:14 22:14 Watch CNBC's full interview with Bill Ackman, Pershing Square CEO President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious. The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants. Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees. Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's " The Morning Meeting " podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision. One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen. "Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said. Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC. In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability. "If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads." MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted. "That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything." Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.

items.title: Mortgage rates have a quiet week as markets digest Fed comments, Trump's directive
items.description: Mortgage rate movement was largely flat in the past week, with the downward momentum of previous weeks cooling off even as more potential homebuyers have been incentivized to seek financing . At HousingWire ’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year loans averaged 7.38% — the same as one week ago . Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.62%, down 7 bps in a week, while 30-year rates for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans stood at 7.16%, down 8 bps. The small declines in rates come a week after the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate at a range of 3.75% of 4% in a widely expected decision . But after policymakers hiked rates in September, further increases are anticipated, with the CME Group ’s FedWatch tool showing that 77% of interest rate traders predict a 25-basis-point increase in December. More details from the Fed HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote this week that tighter monetary policy “has created financial pain for some AI companies.” With the Fed focusing on the inflationary aspects of AI and associated debt-financing issues, the 10-year Treasury yield has been dropping, which has placed downward pressure on mortgage rates. Hector Amendola , president of Las Vegas-based mortgage lender SimplyPMG , told HousingWire in an interview that he believes a December hike is already baked into current rates and that drastic movement, up or down, is unlikely to happen for the rest of this year. “It’s kind of been par for the course now for a while, that rates are continuing to rise based on the expectation that the Fed will go up a little bit more until there’s a way to figure out how to tame inflation a little bit,” Amendola said. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced last week that the central bank would be shifting to fewer policy votes in each of the next two years. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) currently meets eight times a year, with a vote scheduled after each, but the number of votes will be reduced to seven in 2027 and potentially to six in 2028. The move caught Amendola’s eye. “I think it puts a little bit more weight on each of the meetings,” he said. “I also think it’s interesting, because as Warsh kicks over, you’re kind of wondering if it’ll be like, ‘Let’s break everything and see what happens and figure it out later,’ or are we going to continue to really look at the data and do what the data tells us? “I think what I’ve seen so far is, it’s still a wait-and-see approach . Let’s see what the data says, and that’s kind of why I think this particular decision that came out [last week] was expected, because the data is saying, ‘Slow down.’” Reaction to Trump's executive order Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that targets lower costs in multiple areas of housing finance. These include proactive mortgage insurance cancellations for conventional loan servicers, an expanded title waiver program through the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), reduced rates on some government-backed loans and the creation of a manufactured housing task force. Mat Ishbia , president and CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), said this week in his monthly “3 Points” video that “housing affordability continues to be front and center in Washington D.C. There’s a real focus right now on finding ways to lower the cost of homeownership, reduce friction in the mortgage process and make financing more accessible.” He pointed specifically to the proposal to make the title insurance waiver pilot a permanent program, saying that prior waivers on some low-risk refinances have been “saving consumers thousands of dollars.” “Some of these ideas will help; some of them won’t help,” Ishbia said of the executive order. “We’ll see how it all shakes out. But I think these are good things they’re looking at doing.” Amendola said his company has “always been big proponents” of waiving title insurance on refi transactions with loan-to-value ratios below 80%. “Like, what are we really doing? It’s the same consumer. You know, all that stuff is still coming up,” he remarked. He also said that allowing servicers of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans to help borrowers cancel their mortgage insurance premiums when they reach the statutory threshold “is a bigger deal than people think.” U.S. Mortgage Insurers have expressed their support for the move, while some analysts label it as “fairly benign” for the financial performance of mortgage insurers. “That’s extra revenue that they’re making right now that they, honestly, probably shouldn’t be making — and suddenly they’re going to have an impact on their end,” Amendola said. “But it’s going to be really good for the homeowner to free up some of that cash that can then turn into something else for them.” Related More: Donald Trump Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh Mat Ishbia

items.title: Holiday Snow Forecast Reveals Which Lucky Homeowners Will Wake Up to a White Christmas This Year
items.description: November is in full swing, and if you’re starting to map out your holiday travel and winter maintenance game plan ahead of December, The Old Farmer’s Almanac has released its annual snowfall forecast for Christmas Day. While it’s a long-held tradition to hold out hope for a “white” Christmas , this year might not see as many flurries as in years past. It really depends on where you live—and if you do live somewhere with snow in the forecast, the time to secure your home from the elements is now. Dreaming of a White Christmas? With a super El Nino this year, conditions will look incredibly mixed come the holiday season. Loading... Old Farmer's Almanac white Christmas weather forecast for 2026 Old Farmer's Almanac For example, the publication predicts a white Christmas in the Northeast, for places like Vermont and upstate New York . But just below that in New Jersey , Connecticut , and Pennsylvania , there isn’t even a chance of snowfall. Other areas that can bank on snow this Christmas include the Intermountain region (like Colorado and Wyoming), and Alaska , while other regions, including the Pacific Northwest, High Plains, Lower Lakes, and the Ohio Valley, have a "chance of a white Christmas." On the flip side, and perhaps not surprisingly, states in the Atlantic Corridor, the Southeast, Florida , the Deep South, the Upper Midwest, Heartland, Texas - Oklahoma , the Desert Southwest, and the Pacific Southwest are not expected to have a white Christmas Preparing for snow beyond the holiday season Regardless of whether you’re in for a white Christmas, if you live in an area that gets snow, you’ll likely see snow at some point this season. The Farmers' Almanac is advising homeowners to prepare for a winter of “snow, sleet, and surprises” through March 2027. Additionally, according to the NOAA , an El Niño system, like the one that’s been brewing since July, tends to be strongest during the winter months. But because of the strength of the system being tracked this year, there are plenty of variables at play. “Every El Niño is not the same; each one is unique with its own imprint on our weather,” say Ken Graham , director, NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS). "Advanced monitoring and an improved understanding of El Niño patterns allow the NWS to better predict and better prepare the public and our core partners for what is to come.” If a snowstorm is forecasted for your area in the coming months, as a homeowner, there are some important precautions you can take. For starters, pipes leading to outdoor faucets and hoses are particularly vulnerable to damage when the temperature plummets, so it's crucial that you make turning them all off part of prepping for a snowstorm, even if you have little time to spare. So be sure to shut off the inside valves leading out to them, unhook hoses, and run your outdoor faucets to drain any water that might be hiding within. You should also give some thought to your inside pipes to keep them from bursting as well. One smart way to prevent burst pipes indoors, keep cabinet doors under sinks open so warm air in your home can reach them more easily. Also, before a storm settles in, make sure to clean your gutters. Debris in gutters can lead to ice dams, causing roof damage, which is the last thing you want when a storm hits. Finally, a good rule of thumb is to seal any drafty windows. With utility prices as an all-time high, windows become a prime spot for energy loss. “Seal out the cold using a shrink film window kit. This can block drafts and air leaks that lead to high heating costs,” says Randi Bujnovsky , weatherization product manager at Duck , a home weatherization brand in Cleveland . Shrink film window kits are readily available online or at your local home improvement store. Just make sure you read the directions carefully before using one. items.title: Victoria-Marie Mezzanotte
items.description: Victoria-Marie Mezzanotte Realtor EveryPlace with Laughton Team November 03, 2026 What was your most interesting job before going into real estate? I was in adult foster care and teen foster care. I was a direct support professional and assisted in everyday living needs. I love helping others and it’s part of the reason I started real estate to build the connections, community and funds for my own group home facility. Where did you grow up? I grew up here in the Valley. Born and raised born in Glendale and grew up in Peoria, then moved to Buckeye, then to Phoenix, then to Prescott and now I’m back in Buckeye! Growing up, what did you want to be? As a child I wanted to be my own boss and help people who were suffering. I’ve always wanted to have my own group home. What do you do to relax when you’re stressed? I take hot showers, clean my house and read for hours when I have the time! If you could meet any well-known figure (living or not), who would it be and why? What I wouldn’t give to be in the same room as Michio Kaku and Neil deGrasse Tyson. I would have the time of my life talking to them. I’ve always been fascinated by astrophysics, but definitely not smart enough to be an astrophysicist. What is Phoenix's best-kept secret? It’s not really a secret, but the food and the diversity you can find all over the Valley. The best restaurants I’ve ever had have been hidden in areas out of sight. I am a firm believer that smaller businesses have some of the best dining experiences. What do you love most about the industry? The people. You get to converse with some very intelligent people and learn so much if you’re willing to listen. How do you distinguish yourself from the crowd of agents? I don’t think it’s something I have to worry about. My mission and goals speak for themselves, and meeting people in person and getting to talk face to face is always better than what you see online. What is the most difficult aspect of your job? Haha, I can’t say … but making sure to stay true to my values and beliefs is what is most important to me. Sometimes you run into entities who don’t have humanity on their list of priorities and that can be difficult to proceed with. But I believe with great commitment and compassion it can be overcome. What’s your best advice for generating new leads? Having multiple lead-generating sources. As a new agent, being on a good team. Not being afraid to tap into your sphere of influence — sometimes those conversations can be awkward, but with some practice it is beneficial. Not being afraid to have a social media presence. Stepping in front of a camera and speaking with confidence can be scary, but I think it’s a good way to build a platform that shows prospects who you are and what you do. What are you binge-watching/reading/listening to lately? I don’t watch TV, but I’m Gen Z so of course I doom scroll on TikTok. And I love anime — I’m a huge manga and Manhwa nerd. What’s your favorite meal in Phoenix? It’s definitely Manna Grill Korean BBQ in Peoria or Cooper’s Hawk in Avondale. Those are my go-to for any celebration or when I’m feeling like I need to overeat. Architecturally speaking, what is your favorite building in Phoenix? The Orpheum Theatre or The Rosson House Museum. What’s the weirdest thing that’s ever happened to you on the job? Getting calls from weird people after they see my social media posts. That really is bizarre. What’s one thing people are surprised to learn about you? I’m really good at cooking, I’m just so busy nobody ever gets to eat my food! What is your favorite vacation spot and why? I love Newport Beach, California, or the warm waters in Corpus Christi, Texas. It’s much more fun to catch waves that don’t turn your lips blue! What is your favorite city after Phoenix? I’ve always adored the red landscapes of Sedona and the gorgeous properties and architecture there. The green trees make such a beautiful contrast to the red mountains. What is your advice for someone new to the industry? Don’t give up. Keep working hard and grind everyday and you will see success. What’s your favorite real estate iPhone/Android app? Zillow of course! Who are your favorite people to follow on social media? My colleagues and my team pages! Seeing what everyone is doing and hyping each other up. Seeing the content people put hard work into and feeling inspired. What are your social media handles? items.title: Regional MLSs support shared-listing platform Open Real Estate
items.description: Regional MLSs support shared-listing platform Open Real Estate by John Yellig November 02, 2026 Four regional MLSs announced their support for the Open Real Estate shared-listing platform, which was recently rolled out by four of the largest brokerages in the United States to push back against Compass Real Estate’s Private Listing Network . The founders — AGNT Inc., parent of eXp Realty and NextHome; Home Services of America Inc.; Keller Williams Realty LLC, and Real REMAX Group — also noted that the platform had received 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders, and of those, 493 or 59%, came from independent firms. According to the founders, this shows support from brokerages of every size and business model, from single-office independents to some of the largest independent brokerages in the country. Among these are Atlanta Communities, Iron Valley Real Estate, LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America. “We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” the founders said in an announcement. Open Real Estate is designed to complement — and not compete with — existing MLS organizations and aims to work alongside the MLSs to expand access to listings for brokerages, agents and consumers, founders said. “Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” NorthstarMLS President and CEO Tim Dain said. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.” “We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” Bright MLS President and CEO Brian Donnellan said. “[North Texas Real Estate Information Systems] remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative and neutral marketplace that serves all broker participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service,” said NTREIS CEO Chris Carrillo “Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform,” CRMLS CEO Art Carter said. “It has been a long-term project of CRMLS to allow our brokers to have that ability. items.title: Inspector general hits Pulte over 'unprecedented' obstruction
items.description: Inspector general hits Pulte over 'unprecedented' obstruction By Katy O'Donnell and Erin Schilling Published November 03, 2026, 10:52 a.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email The nation's top housing regulator took "unprecedented" steps to hinder investigations by its inspector general, the watchdog told lawmakers in a report published Monday. Processing Content The accusations – delivered in the Office of Inspector General's semiannual report to Congress – are the latest escalation in a feud between Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte and his congressionally mandated overseers. Pulte announced on social media in September that he would be slashing the OIG budget by more than 60%. The FHFA regulates Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the government-owned mortgage companies with $7.8 trillion in assets underpinning the mortgage market. Its inspector general is charged with policing mortgage fraud that could pose risk to their portfolios. It is also the office charged with investigating potential improprieties by agency leadership. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte Eric Lee/Bloomberg "OIG's Office of Evaluations was unable to publish three reports" over the six months ending Sept. 30 "due to FHFA's refusal to provide enterprise records and information when requested," according to the report. Fannie and Freddie are sometimes called government-sponsored enterprises. But FHFA spokesman Jonathan Coppage said that the agency had "delivered every document and engaged in every interview the IG has requested under its statutory authorities." "FHFA has readily produced the hundreds of pages of documents and engaged in hours of interviews that the OIG requested regarding FHFA's oversight of Fannie and Freddie multifamily business," Coppage added. "For example, for just three recent reviews we completed 56 document requests and 16 separate hour-long meetings." In an unusual letter to lawmakers hours after Pulte announced the sweeping budget cuts on Sept. 30, Acting Principal Deputy Inspector General James Hodge said the office would be forced to cut up to 80% of its staff and end most criminal inquiries. That decision will have "devastating consequences," the new report concludes. "The unprecedented and abrupt cuts will prevent OIG from conducting meaningful oversight of FHFA going forward." Coppage pointed out that the inspector general had requested a budget much larger than those of other inspectors general. "Independence does not mean exemption from fiscal accountability," he said. "FHFA remains willing to work with OIG to offer what support it needs to effectively budget and exercise reasonable financial stewardship in carrying out its statutory responsibilities, as is customary in every federal agency." Hodge has maintained that the housing regulator watchdog is different from similar offices at other agencies because of the "enormous risks to the U.S. financial system inherent in the operations" of the entities FHFA regulates. Agency leadership has also "eviscerated" the inspector general's ability to investigate and deter mortgage and bank fraud, according to the report. OIG investigations over the past six months recovered $29 million and resulted in 46 indictments. Reuters earlier reported the OIG report, which was delivered to lawmakers Friday. items.title: Angel Oak posts 3Q GAAP loss as non-QM becomes challenging
items.description: Angel Oak posts 3Q GAAP loss as non-QM becomes challenging By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 03, 2026, 2:01 p.m. EST | Updated November 03, 2026, 7:46 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content Expert Quote: "During the quarter, non-QM and the fixed income market became more challenging" — Sreeni Prabhu, CEO and president Supporting Data: A $24 million hit to earnings from the company's securitization portfolio. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Distributable earnings for the third quarter Angel Oak Mortgage REIT were below estimates because of lower than expected net interest income, although the total economic return for the company's stock was better than BTIG's forecast, its post-earnings report said. On a GAAP basis, the non-qualified mortgage securitizer lost $16.7 million, compared with $3.4 million of net income in the second quarter and $11.4 million one year prior. The primary driver was a $24 million hit related to realized and unrealized net losses in its securitization portfolio, Brandon Filson, chief financial officer, said on the earnings call. How Angel Oak compared with other mREITs The BTIG report noted the consensus for distributable earnings was 4 cents per share over what Angel Oak reported. The REIT came in at 28 cents per share, and when realized gains on rate hedges are excluded, the miss to BTIG was 5 cents per share. "AOMR's economic book value performance is below the peer average of residential credit mREITs that have reported third-quarter book value so far, though we would note there is a wide range of 3Q book value performance (+2% to -20%)," wrote Douglas Harter, managing director at BTIG. Angel Oak's management said its business in the quarter was affected by macro factors in the market. Factors which impacted Angel Oak's results "During the quarter, non-QM and the fixed income market became more challenging as higher rates and a shift upward in the yield curve pressured asset valuation and compressed financing spreads across [the] mortgage credit market," said Sreeni Prabhu, CEO and president, on the earnings call. "While this environment negatively impacted book values across the landscape, as expected, Angel Oak's underlying credit performance of her portfolio remained stable and continued to perform in line with our expectations." Sreeni Prabhu, president and CEO at Angel Oak Mortgage REIT. Any valuation pressure reflects what is happening in the broader markets than any deterioration in credit quality or the underlying mortgage performance, which is an important distinction, Prabhu said. The REIT completed two securitizations in the quarter, before the height of the increase in interest rates. It has offered one so far in the current period, which Prabhu said was to mitigate further rate risk. Current market conditions are affecting Angel Oak's buying Lately, non-QM production has declined and the higher interest rate environment compressed returns on new investment. But Angel Oak is continuing to buy loans which meet its credit and return criteria. "We remain deliberate in pacing of our capital deployment across loan businesses and disciplined in maintaining underwriting standards that are central to our strategy, rather than extending risk and pursuing incremental returns at the expense of long-term credit performance," Prabhu said. However, a Bank of America Securities report from Oct. 30 noted the strong growth in non-QM originations which have come to market has not been reflected in the rate lock data. "We think this has to do with the increase in non-QM originators, with already more than 50 new originators in 2026," the report from Pratik Gupta, Chris Flanagan and Andy Fan said. "Either way, there is likelihood that rate lock is still underestimating the amount of supply that the non-QM market will see for this year and the beginning of 2027." Through Oct. 30, $100 million of non-QM issuance has been made during 2026 , up from $59 million at the start of July, B of A said. During the Q&A, Filson noted that typically these mortgages take 30-to-60 days to go through the lock process before they are closed and ready for securitization. Current returns are not quite as good as Angel Oak expects but they are starting to recover, he continued. But if the rate environment stays where it is, the set of locks the REIT gets through the next month will be back at return levels it expects. Management was asked about the state of the market, particularly if it is seeing more home equity line of credit business versus non-QM. From Angel Oak's perspective, the non-QM market remains strong, Filson said. In July, Angel Oak did a HELOC securitization with a current balance of $221.4 million. After the issuance, "we pulled back a little bit on the HELOC purchasing for the quarter, so we didn't really purchase too many in the quarter," Filson said. "But that's a switch and a valve that we could turn on and off very easily." Brad Finkelstein Originations Editor Brad Finkelstein is the originations editor of National Mortgage News. items.title: Real estate is moving toward more data privacy. Appraisers say UAD 3.6 is moving the other way
items.description: Monday marks the implementation date of UAD 3.6 , which requires appraisers to select specific data points from dropdown menus for every feature of a property, as opposed to writing text descriptions of the home as they previously did, increasing the amount of detail included in appraisal reports delivered to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . Within UAD 3.6 is the new Certification 25, which has generated quite the buzz among appraisal professionals. Certification 25, which was established by the government sponsored entities (GSEs), expands the data reuse beyond the parameters set in UAD 2.6, which included Certification 21, which largely governed who could receive or distribute a physical appraisal report. Under Certification 25, entities that receive appraisal reports like lenders, GSEs, secondary market participants and data collection services to store, copy, reproduce, analyze, use and distribute all data within the report, including interior photos and property details, for internal or external purposes without needing the appraiser's further consent. While the certification does state that the appraiser and supervisory appraiser bear no liability for any use of the report outside of the specific mortgage finance transaction, appraisers are still concerned about this change and how it could impact their relationship with brokerages and real estate professionals. In posts on social media and articles written on Appraisers Blog, Desiree Mehbod, a Virginia-based appraiser, has raised concerns about what would happen if interior photos of a child’s bedroom with the property address are leaked, reproduced and shared, ultimately ending up on the dark web. “The biggest issue [with UAD 3.6] is Certification 25, which forces us to legally sign off that any downstream entity can permanently store, analyze, distribute and harvest our entire report data without our consent,” Mehbod told HousingWire . “Data privacy is incredibly important to people when it comes to their intimate spaces like bedrooms and bathrooms. When homeowners realize that the interior photos we take of their private living areas are being distributed to a long list of unknown third parties and permanent corporate tech archives, that trust is completely shattered.” Data privacy vs. data distribution For appraisers like Mehbod, it is noteworthy that these changes are coming at a time when privacy is becoming a hot topic among real estate professionals and consumers. From consumers asking their agents to remove listings photos from the internet after the sale of a home and the rise in private listings networks to MLS seeking to rein in who can use listing data and how , it seems that everyone wants increased data privacy and protection, but appraisers say Certification 25 is doing the opposite of that. “The listing side is building walls to protect consumer privacy, while the appraisal side is being forced to demand more data to feed a permanent corporate tech archive,” Mehbod said. “Reconciling this requires giving independent appraisers the exact same granular data controls and licensing protections that Realtors now have.” But the ability for downstream actors to have access to data like this is not new. According to Frank Gregoire, a Florida-based appraiser, Certification 25 is fairly similar to the statute it is replacing, Certification 21. “Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac maintain a proprietary database about every single dwelling that has ever had a loan on it,” Gregoire said. “So, the ability for downstream users to have access to that data has been there since these forms were introduced in the early 2000s. But, what is new is that it now specifies that the appraiser is aware that some parties may be using the data from their reports without their permission.” Who is getting this information? While Ryan Lundquist agrees that this is the only primary change with Certification 25, he still finds it incredibly concerning. “They can take the information and share it with whoever they want and the appraiser doesn’t have any control over that,” Lundquist, a Sacramento-based appraiser, said. "I know a lot of appraisers feel conflicted about that as it feels like it puts appraisers in a tough spot where a blank check to mine whatever data they want exists.” Lundquist said he would love to know who this information will be shared with or sold to. Gregoire is also concerned about appraisers including copyrighted data, such as images in the MLS in their report. “If the appraiser is an MLS participant, they are using that information under license and they are permitted to use it to support their valuation, but that is it, they cannot grant someone else the right to use that information and that is what's happening with Certification 25,” he said. Just the beginning for Certification 25? It is concerns like these that lead appraisers to say the discussion around Certification 25 is not over yet. “I don’t think it will sit well with a lot of people in real estate when they read or begin to understand how and where this data may be used,” Lundquist said. In addition, Mehbod said Certification 25 is why she and other like-minded appraisers have chosen to stop doing appraisal work for the GSEs. If a homebuyer wants their loan to close they have no choice but to allow the appraiser to generate a report, which Mehbod said will create “massive animosity right at the front door.” “It positions the appraiser as a forced data collector rather than an independent expert,” she said. “This friction damages public trust and opens a legal minefield for our profession, leaving appraisers highly vulnerable to consumer complaints and lawsuits from angry borrowers when transactions get messy over data harvesting policies they never wanted to participate in.” With UAD 3.6 just beginning to go into effect, it remains to be seen if anything regarding Certification 25 will change or how consumers and real estate brokers, agents and MLSs will respond. items.title: Social Security COLA, tax break could narrow spending gap for older consumers in 2027
items.description: The spending growth of older consumers has trailed other age groups for the past year despite sizable wealth gains at the top. But a 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security recipients and temporary tax break could modestly improve their purchasing power, according to a Bank of America Institute report released last week. Bank of America aggregated credit and debit card data to show that baby boomer and traditionalist households have posted weaker discretionary spending growth than other Americans for roughly a year. That marks a reversal from 2022 and 2023, when older households were outpacing others. Boomers were defined as those born between 1946 and 1964, while traditionalists are those born before 1946. The report ties part of this slowdown to how wealth is distributed within the older cohorts. Using 2025 data from the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, the bank found that about two-thirds of net wealth among households headed by someone older than 65 is held by the top 10% of these households. This concentration means that stock market and asset gains may do little to support spending for most older consumers. Labor income boom skips many retirees Overall consumer spending strength in 2026 appears to be driven primarily by wage and salary growth , particularly among lower- and middle-income working households. Older households, by contrast, depend on a broader mix of income sources and are less exposed to accelerating wages. Fed survey data shows that as households age, a smaller share of income comes from wages or self-employment and more from pensions, Social Security, and interest, dividends or rental income . Bank of America’s internal data highlight the resulting divergence within older cohorts: Households over 62 that rely only on Social Security have average income and discretionary spending close to half that of their peers who drawing from Social Security, pensions and employment combined. Discretionary spending is also more uneven across income tiers for older generations than for all households. Retirees are the least likely group to expect their finances to improve over the next six months, according to the study , reflecting the challenges of living on largely fixed income sources. Policy supports: tax deduction and 2027 COLA The report points to two policy levers that could support older consumers’ budgets in the near term: Temporary tax deduction: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act , signed last year, provides a temporary deduction of up to $6,000 for each taxpayer age 65 or older from 2025 to 2028. The benefit phases out above $75,000 of modified adjusted gross income for single filers and $150,000 for joint filers. Bank of America says this should lift after-tax income and spending capacity mainly for middle-income older households that have meaningful federal tax liability. Social Security COLA: The Social Security Administration has announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, effective in January. That is the largest COLA since 2023 but smaller than the 8.7% increase in 2022. COLAs are based on the year-over-year change in the third quarter for the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). While these increases are designed to preserve purchasing power, they can be more or less generous depending on the inflation path in the year that follows. In 2022, for example, inflation slowed sharply after a large COLA took effect, effectively boosting real benefits and helping older generations outspend other age cohorts in 2022 and 2023. Consensus forecasts cited in the Bank of America report anticipate that overall inflation will cool in 2027, largely as the impact of higher gasoline prices fades. If that occurs, the 3.6% COLA could outpace actual price increases next year, delivering a more meaningful real income gain for households heavily reliant on Social Security. Why this matters for housing The survey data shows that the largest spending growth gaps between older generations and all households are concentrated in discretionary categories like electronics, lodging, restaurants, clothing, furniture and airlines. In many of these areas, older cohorts’ year-over-year spending growth lags the overall population by several percentage points. Some of this pattern likely reflects differences in preferences and life stages. But if Social Security benefits rise faster than prices in 2027 and the tax deduction continues to support middle-income seniors, the report suggests there may be room for older households’ discretionary spending growth to narrow the gap with other age groups. Slower discretionary spending among older Americans, combined with highly concentrated wealth, underscores the financial pressures on many households that are past their peak earning years. For housing professionals, this has several implications: Senior housing demand mix: Modest real income gains in 2027 may support demand for lower-cost aging-in-place solutions , repairs and modifications rather than large discretionary moves or high-end rentals. Retirement cash-flow planning: Mortgage lenders and real estate agents who work with older buyers and sellers should factor in the role of Social Security COLAs and targeted tax provisions when assessing affordability , especially for those on fixed incomes. Segmented strategies: With income and spending highly diverse within the 62-plus segment, professionals will need to tailor products and marketing differently for asset-rich, higher-income retirees versus Social Security-dependent households. Bank of America stresses that its findings are based on anonymized, aggregated transaction and survey data and should be considered alongside broader economic indicators. items.title: Real Brokerage expands in Midwest with Iowa-based The Team
items.description: The Real Brokerage announced that real estate leaders Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit have moved their 30-agent brokerage to Real under the name The Team . The group, based in Dubuque, Iowa , previously operated as an independent brokerage known as Unlimited . The Team serves buyers and sellers across Dubuque; Galena, Illinois; and southern Wisconsin. Since 2020, the brokerage has closed about 5,000 transactions totaling $1.2 billion in volume, according to the company announcement. The move gives Real , a top-ranked firm by RealTrends Verified , a larger foothold in a smaller but active Midwest market as national brokerages continue to compete for productive teams rather than individual agents. For brokers and team leaders, these platform moves can signal shifting economics around splits, stock incentives, technology stacks and administrative support. Buchheit brings more than 30 years of real estate experience to Real and also co-owns multiple complementary businesses in property management, insurance, HVAC, cleaning and construction. That ecosystem can create cross-sales and referral opportunities while helping to stabilize revenue through market cycles. Buchheit recruited Burger to Unlimited in 2020 to run the company, a partnership that preceded Unlimited’s merger with the region’s largest brokerage. Together they grew Unlimited into a local market leader by both agent count and production, the announcement explained. Burger has balanced ownership responsibilities with active production. He is on track to generate about $15 million in personal sales volume in 2026, according to the announcement. At Real, Burger and Buchheit plan to leverage the firm’s cloud-based brokerage platform to streamline operations, recruit additional agents and expand into new Midwest markets. “Cody and Dennis have built a business with a strong regional presence and a clear vision for growth,” Joel Kirsch, senior vice president of growth at Real and a 2024 HousingWire Insider , said in the announcement. “They bring valuable operational experience, production success and an entrepreneurial mindset.” Buchheit said the switch was driven largely by technology and long-term positioning. “Real is light-years ahead when it comes to technology and where the industry is going,” he said, noting that the platform and community provide tools and relationships to “build a business that’s positioned for the future.” Burger said the move will allow him to spend less time on day-to-day management and more time on production, agent development and geographic expansion. “I’ve spent years running every aspect of the business while still producing, and Real gives me an opportunity to take a lot off my plate,” he said. items.title: Rocket attacks broker conversion issues with new tool
items.description: Rocket attacks broker conversion issues with new tool By Colin McNamara Published November 03, 2026, 2:43 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Rocket Pro is launching a tool that will help mortgage brokers address conversion issues, as the lender continues its efforts to gain more wholesale business. Processing Content Part of Rocket's monthly Power Play initiative, the new app called Quick Counter allows brokers to build, adjust and deliver a competitive refinance loan estimate while the client is still on the phone, the company announced Tuesday. It will help loan officers avoid losing momentum due to callbacks. Austin Niemiec, Rocket chief revenue officer "The product itself is attacking the problem around conversion, especially in a really tough market ," Austin Niemiec, chief revenue officer at Rocket, told National Mortgage News. "Brokers can use Quick Counter to adjust the options and then deliver a real loan estimate that ensures they're competitive and they can win without stepping away from the conversation." The app builds on Rocket's investment in its wholesale channel and, similar to October's announcement, is a more permanent fixture in the lender's benefits for brokers. Last month, Rocket rolled out its Orbit platform, which provides brokers with advantages and perks that help them compete, ranging from more certainty on purchase loans to pricing flexibility when a deal needs help. Rocket also extended the pricing credit its broker partners can receive by working with a Compass buyer's agent . The partnership has generated $3 billion in rate locks since it was announced in February, the company said. "We are using our all-weather strength as a company to continue to invest and deliver value to brokers," Niemiec said. "These things are building off each other as a strategy where brokers take our technology and then take our fantastic pricing and use them to be more competitive and move faster when it comes to converting loans." The full launch included: The Quick Counter app built into Rocket Pro Navigate, the company's artificial intelligence hub for brokers; Live loan estimate generation for cash-out and rate-and-term refinances; Real-time adjustments to rates, points and loan terms; Options to evaluate lowest closing. Rocket doesn't yet have an estimate on the tool's expected effectiveness, but believes it will be one of the most used within Rocket Pro Navigate, Niemiec said. Quick Counter was West Capital Lending Broker Seth Hasan's winning idea from The Big Pitch competition at Rocket Pro's RPX event in September. "This was developed by a broker, voted by the entire broker community, and then we worked side by side with Seth and his team to make sure that we were bringing their vision to life," Niemiec said. items.title: 7 Year-End Tax Planning Tips to Help Businesses and Individuals Prepare for 2027
items.description: Live Poll As 2026 winds down, business owners and individuals may be looking for ways to reduce their tax bills before the calendar flips. But according to Joe Lavis , Partner-in-Charge of the Dallas Office and Tax Partner at Whitley Penn , effective year-end tax planning isn't necessarily about finding the biggest deduction. It's about understanding where you stand financially, anticipating what's ahead and making decisions that strengthen your broader financial picture--not just the year in the rearview mirror. That could mean reviewing your investment portfolio, reevaluating a planned business purchase or simply having a conversation with your CPA before it's too late to make meaningful changes, charitable giving or strategic investments. And with a myriad of tax law changes affecting everything from business deductions to charitable contributions stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill, taking a closer look before Dec. 31 could be especially valuable this year. Here are seven considerations Lavis says businesses and individuals should keep in mind as they close out 2026 and prepare for 2027. Joe Lavis is the Partner-in-Charge of the Dallas Office and Tax Partner at Whitley Penn. 1. Know where you stand before making any moves Knowing what needs to happen as 2026 comes to a close starts with knowing where you currently stand. "The most important first step is understanding where you stand at this point in the year," Lavis explained. "Pull everything together in a spreadsheet so you can identify planning opportunities and get a clearer picture of what's ahead for your 2026 taxes." Taxpayers, whether individuals or businesses, should be looking to identify how much they've paid up to this point relative to how much they estimate they may owe, which can help determine their tax position. If the year-end projection shows a balance due, you may want to consider adjusting your withholding or estimated payments, depending on your circumstances, to avoid a similar result in 2027. Depending on your goals, cash flow and eligibility, you may also want to evaluate Q4 strategies such as qualified charitable giving or investments in needed business assets that could reduce your tax liability and better position you for 2027. 2. Review opportunities to reduce taxable income Once you understand your current status, that's when you can figure out what moves to make in the final months of the year. Lavis said some of the most common opportunities for individuals include making tax-advantaged retirement contributions, while businesses may be able to take advantage of provisions such as bonus depreciation, which allows a 100% write-off for eligible business-use assets. "You shouldn't be on your own in this journey because it can be very complicated," Lavis said. "There's a lot of misinformation out there--the tax code gets more complicated each year, and while some of the technology and AI is great out there, it can also lead you down the wrong road. If you're relying on some of that information, just one minor detail can throw off an assumption that you've made in your tax planning. "Additionally, AI can make unseen assumptions based on the prompt you're providing or a misinterpretation of information it thinks it knows already, which can cause downstream miscalculations," he added. "It's also important that the most recent regulation is what your AI searches are referencing. Don't let AI hallucinations impact your livelihood." Effective tax planning involves more than reducing tax liability. It also means evaluating cash flow, business expenses and long-term financial goals. (Photo by Vitaly Gariev via Pexels) 3. Don't spend money just to save on taxes While it can be easy to get caught up in the current year, Lavis explained that it's more important to think long-term, especially for businesses. "I think the biggest misconception is that the only angle is driving down tax dollars," Lavis explained. "Tax is a very important factor in decision making, but it's not the only factor. At the end of the day, cash is everything." "So, for instance, if you're at the end of the year and you're looking to reduce taxes and you're a business and you go out and buy equipment that you don't need, that's great because you get the deduction, but then you've spent a dollar to save 40 cents," he added. "You've got to make sure that you're accounting for all the asset needs of the business, financial situations and reasoning, not just through the tax lens." 4. Factor in major financial changes from 2026 A particularly strong or weak year can impact a business in the same way a major life event can impact an individual when it comes to taxes. "A successful year typically means more cash, so you've got more opportunities there to do some tax advantageous strategy and planning. In a weaker year, you obviously don't want to rely on the strategies that you use in a stronger year," Lavis noted. These instances are where a CPA can really help guide you in the right direction--but only if you loop them in as soon as possible and keep strong records. "The earlier that you're able to get this information over to your CPA, the better that you can plan for it. If you sold your business in October, and then you tell your CPA on Dec. 31, there's not a whole lot we can do other than acknowledge you're going to owe a lot of taxes," Lavis said. "The quicker you can turn this information over to your CPA, the quicker you can game plan for it. That's why it's important for that relationship with your CPA to have this open line of communication," he added. Working with a CPA throughout the year can help business owners navigate changing tax regulations, identify deductions and plan for future financial needs. (Photo by Vitaly Gariev via Pexels) 5. items.description: A California man convinced dozens of investors to pour millions of dollars into a real estate venture he claimed would deliver big returns through the construction of backyard homes. But the 30-year-old accountant lost more than $8.2 million of their money in risky stock market trades and not a single accessory dwelling unit (ADU) was built, prosecutors said. Ethan Joseph Sanchez , of San Diego, was sentenced to 63 months in federal prison after admitting to orchestrating the investment fraud scheme , the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of California announced Friday. “Ethan Sanchez exploited the trust of hardworking people and stole their savings through lies and fabricated investments,” U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon said in a statement. “This sentence reflects the profound harm he caused.” Sanchez, who was a certified public accountant at the time and operated through his business, BSC Equity Ventures LLC., repeatedly lied to his victims as to how their investment funds would be used, according to prosecutors. The scheme began back in 2022 when Sanchez allegedly began soliciting loans from investors, falsely claiming the money would fund real estate ventures, including the construction and renovation of ADUs. He promised the investors they would receive their principal back as soon as possible, with an above-average return of interest, in some cases as much as 25%. Sanchez also allegedly used a fictitious identity, Richard “Rick” Aguilar, to make the investment opportunities appear more legitimate. But prosecutors say Sanchez used the investors’ funds for day trading and in most cases lost the money. He did not fund the real estate transactions he said the investors were financing nor did he build any of the ADUs he said would be financed with the investors’ money. Loading... Ethan Sanchez allegedly told investors that the money would be used for real estate transactions, specifically for the construction of ADUs. An Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) is a small, separate living space on the same property as a single-family home Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety The FBI reported in February 2025 that BSC Equity Ventures had received over $6 million in investments from its investors, while Sanchez returned less than $1.8 million to them. At the sentencing hearing on Oct. 30, U.S. District Judge Robert S. Huie ordered Sanchez to forfeit over $8.2 million and to pay restitution to victims. He described the scheme as “aggravated and reprehensible,” highlighting how Sanchez had used existing victims to recruit additional investors, sometimes including members of their own families. The judge described the harm caused by the scheme as “almost unimaginable,” adding that the consequences went far beyond the financial losses. In a January 2026 interview with ABC 10News , one investor, identified only as Brooke , said the loss he suffered forced him out of retirement and back to work to rebuild his savings. Brooke told the outlet that Sanchez told him he needed money to refinance his portfolio of investment properties and would pay interest on the loans. Sanchez initially borrowed $40,000 from Brooke in December 2023, but then continued to borrow more money, including a $150,000 loan. Sanchez made small payments, Brooke said, but never repaid the full amount of his investment. Brooke also said that he had borrowed against his home to make the investment with Sanchez and was paying interest on that money. “It was always lie after lie,” he said. “And then it became so obvious that this was a Ponzi scheme.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now

items.title: Chris Pratt Says He Was ‘Living in a Van’ With ‘About $60’ Before Big Hollywood Break
items.description: “Guardians of the Galaxy” actor Chris Pratt may be enjoying a lavish life as a movie star these days—but before he achieved major success in Hollywood , he was a restaurant server living humbly in Hawaii . In an Oct. 29 post shared on X , the “Jurassic World” actor , 47, opened up about the unlikely encounter that turned it all around. “Before Hollywood, I was living in a van in Hawaii and waiting tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp Company. One day, the incredible Rae Dawn Chong walked into the restaurant, and naturally, I went up to her table and said, ‘Hey, you’re a movie star! What are you doing here?’” he wrote. When Chong, who starred in “The Color Purple,” asked Pratt if he could act, he recalled replying, “F-ck yeah, put me in your movie!” From there, Chong asked for Pratt’s phone number. Loading... Chris Pratt is sharing the unlikely story of the moment Rae Dawn Chong gave him his big Hollywood break. Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images Loading... Before making it big as an actor, Pratt was "living in a van" in Hawaii. Today, he lives in Los Angeles with his wife, Katherine Schwarzenegger. Amy Sussman/Getty Images “The only problem was I didn’t have one,” he said. “So I gave her my buddy Mike’s number instead.” Pratt explained that “a couple days later,” his friend “casually” mentioned that someone had called looking for him. Pratt returned Chong’s call and discovered that her offer was legitimate. “I drove over to pick up the script, went back to Mike’s house, and read all 120 pages three times in a row,” Pratt wrote, sharing that it was the first script he’d ever read. “My character’s name was Devon, and I remember thinking, ‘Sweet! I could totally play a Devon!’” The father of four prepared extensively for the audition, which worked well in his favor. “Rae told me I could act and offered me the part. I asked if we were shooting in Hawaii. Nope. Los Angeles,” he wrote. Loading... Pratt and Schwarzenegger have been trying to sell their Pacific Palisades mansion since 2023. Realtor.com Loading... The home has been put on the market five times without snagging a buyer. Realtor.com Loading... The couple first asked $32 million for the home in July 2023. It's now listed at $19.99 million after a series of price cuts. Realtor.com With just “about $60” to his name, “a bag of clothes, and some rollerblades,” Pratt sensed his situation would be changing soon. “Then Rae told me they’d fly me out. And I remember thinking right then and there, my life just changed forever,” he wrote. “I’m going to be an actor.” Pratt remarked he will “forever be grateful to Rae for taking a chance on a kid working at a shrimp restaurant,” adding that the “little movie” that gave him his start was the 2000 film “Cursed: Part III”—a project he described as “a low-budget horror comedy. That opened the door to Hollywood for me.” The actor’s living arrangements have been given quite the upgrade in the years since he was staying in a van. Pratt and his wife, Katherine Schwarzenegger , 36, are reportedly residing in a Montecito property that was previously home to pop star Katy Perry as they try to offload their sprawling Pacific Palisades mansion. The couple has been trying to sell for years, after purchasing the property in June 2018 for $15.6 million and razing the existing home to build the custom 13,000-square-foot megamansion that currently stands. The price has been slashed a few times since they initially listed it for $32 million in July 2023, and it currently sits at $19.99 million—the lowest price it has been, in its fifth time on the market in three years. The listing, which is held by Shana Tavangarian of Carolwood Estates, describes the six-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom abode as a “one of a kind architectural masterpiece” that was created “with no expense spared.” Boasting “luxury quality construction” and “grand scale and volume throughout,” the estate is located on just under an acre within a “boutique gated community” While it was initially understood that the property had been intended to serve as the couple's permanent family home, they ended up purchasing another mansion for $12.5 million in 2023, this time opting for a parcel that is just a stone's throw from the Brentwood house of Schwarzenegger's mother, Maria Shriver . Again, they demolished the dwelling that stood on that parcel in order to begin construction on another custom manse, which they broke ground on in 2024. Their most recent construction project has already sparked furious controversy , however, after it was revealed that Pratt and Schwarzenegger had demolished a midcentury modern property designed by acclaimed architect Craig Ellwood in order to make way for their new custom dwelling. Design fans were upset by the couple's decision to tear down the original structure, known as the Zimmerman House, which dated to the 1950s and was considered a design gem. Work on that property is still understood to be ongoing—and it appears that, while they wait for their latest home to be completed, Pratt and Schwarzenegger are continuing to reside in the Montecito property once owned by Perry and her former fiancé, Orlando Bloom .
