items.title: The Founder of Sky Rocket Has a New Bar—and a Thrilling New Burger
items.description: Live Poll Scott Wagner has a screw loose. That’s his immediate answer, at least, to the question, “Why open a restaurant again?” We’re talking on day three since he quietly opened the doors to his new burger-and-chicken-tenders joint , Swaggy’s, on Preston Road in North Dallas. (Important: it’s in the same strip mall as Deli News.) Wagner is already dropping a smashed cheeseburger with a charred-to-crunchy cap that’ll put stars in your eyes. Entertainment Restaurant Review: The Best Pastrami Sandwich in Dallas at Deli-News By Nancy Nichols | March 8, 2012 | 11:44 am Wagner could've easily sat back and let his previous restaurant keep cruising its franchising tour around the city. Maybe you’ve heard of it: Sky Rocket Burger . Eight years ago , in a strip mall under the howling George Bush turnpike (the view from the front door was an ExxonMobil station), Wagner changed his job status from car salesman to burger joint owner. Sky Rocket’s first round of cheeseburgers, fired on a four-foot griddle (there was barely room in the kitchen at the time), was no sales trick: simple, true-blue flavors from a brisket-beef blend patty, seasoned with just salt and pepper, made it one of the best hole-in-the-wall, red plastic basket cheeseburgers in the city. Today, Sky Rocket has five locations, with one more on the way. Wagner remains a Sky Rocket partner. But he isn’t a “sit back” kind of guy. “Look down the street,” he says. “Which two restaurants have lines? In-N-Out and Raising Cane’s. I want to marry those two.” Like a celebrity invited to the Swift-Kelce ceremony, I'm publicly all in on this union. Are you tired of smash burgers yet? If you are, hang in there — we’ve got one more for you to devour. Wagner’s entry into the trend is an instant stunner, crowned with a dark, charred cap on one side of the patty. A single bite reveals a thick, crackly crunch. Onions, long-simmered into a jam, are spread over the patty before it gets that hard, hissing sear. It’s also just over eight bucks. Mercifully, this isn't a lacy-thin patty, screamingly smashed on the griddle until it looks like someone blasted it with a shotgun. Swaggy’s is a thicker patty, once more, made with a brisket-beef blend. The first burger on the menu, the Classic Onion Smash, proudly wears the yellowest-yellow Mr. American Cheese. Just pickles, a tangy mayo-blend sauce, and a lightly toasted potato bun surround the patty. The rest of the menu riffs on this burger, including a “Texican” with jalapeños and chorizo, a BBQ sauce-bacon-onion ring variation, and an aorta-clencher with two chicken tenders on two slices of pepper. Then there’s his Raising Cane’s competition tender. His regular and spicy tenders have thin, crisp shells and a lighter batter (think fish and chips), without thick, craggy edges, and they're juicier and brighter than your usual tender. His chicken tender dipping sauce is another shot across the Raising Cane’s bow, a Rocky vs. Apollo entry, with tangy-creamy mayo, ketchup, and other lock-and-key seasonings. A surprise left hook: the tenders are available as a sandwich, which, I’m calling now, will soon be part of an influencer’s “come with me” tour of the place. Despite executing simple foods with finesse, Wagner doesn't see himself as a chef. A chef makes him think of the classic French tweezering and things “en croûte,” he tells me. Wagner just wants a place that’s a good hang. Swaggy’s setup is more elevated than Sky Rocket, lined with dark walls, softer lighting, and clean, modern lines surrounding the in-progress bar. Flatscreen TVs with the game on and such. One thing’s for sure: Wagner knows how to smash a burger, and that’s worth hanging around. items.title: The Dallas Opera's Newest Triumph Is Part Fable, Part Comedy, All Surprises
items.description: Live Poll Sometimes a night at the opera means high melodrama and emotions as big as the sets. Sometimes it can be a comic time capsule of jokes people found funny 200 years ago. The Dallas Opera’s current production defies every expectation. It’s one of the very rare shows where the story, cast, production, and music come together to produce their own all-new thrill. It is, for much of the short 100-minute runtime, pure magic, maybe the most fun I’ve ever had at an opera house. The Cunning Little Vixen , a Czech-language opera by Leoš Janáček, is based on newspaper comics. It tells the story of a fox in the woods who is caught by a forester and brought home to keep his dog company. I don’t want to spoil the many surprises that follow, but let’s just say that the fox isn’t tamed, many more animals will show up, and love will break out. The story is deeply silly, but the Dallas Opera producers and actors give total commitment. Guides Our Top Event Picks for the Weekend How to enjoy local arts, music, culture, food, fitness, and more all week long in Dallas. By Kataeya Sharp , Bethany Erickson | October 29, 2026 | 9:00 am The opera seizes our imagination because it defies our expectations. The plot may be about cute animals, but it’s not for young children. There are fable-like elements but no clear moral. The story is funny but with serious human emotions are heart. Most of the talent for this production—singers, acrobats, director, and designers—is making their Dallas debuts, with an instant, electric chemistry. Janáček’s opera comes from 1923 but his music is particularly well-suited to our time. With irrepressible rhythms, insistent repeated motifs, and the occasional heart-melting romantic gesture, he sets a kinetic pace and rarely slows down. Janáček in some ways invented musical minimalism, but his vision is different from, say, Philip Glass’: he lets tunes mutate, distort, and volley across the stage. When a poacher stalks the woods, trombones and tuba snarl with menace. The music is constantly thrilling, though some singers in minor roles struggle to be heard over the orchestra. (Not a problem for soprano Mirjam Mesak as the fox or Zachary Nelson, the excellent forester. By the way, anyone who’s ever owned a pet will recognize the way Mesak's fox dashes around the stage hyperactively, then takes a quick nap.) The composer took the unusual step of writing his own story and lyrics, which are quite modern. Janáček demands gender swaps for some roles, wink-hints at a feminist animal kingdom, and supplies one witticism I plan to recycle endlessly. One character asks, “How are you?” The other says, “I would be very well indeed, but for all my troubles.” Isn’t that the truth? The Dallas Opera production, a collaboration with opera companies in Munich and Barcelona, reimagines the staging to be as timeless as the words and plot. Gone are specific forest sets, henhouses, and bird nests; in their place are glittering abstract sets of exceptional beauty. Original director Barrie Kosky wants us to see the story as a comic parable, not a literal tale of adorable critters. Minimalist set design makes the tavern feel like a pretty bleak place. Zachary Nelson (left) gets his drinks from innkeeper Johnny Brown. Kyle Flubacker / courtesy The Dallas Opera A significant fault with Kosky’s abstracted staging is that sometimes the viewer simply does not know who is who. Human characters all dress in black, but the “animals” wear any human clothing they want, pajamas included. In one of the very first scenes, the Forester tries to sleep while one adult and a gaggle of children do their best to irritate him. Who are they? The program book and Wikipedia tell me that one is a mosquito and another is a frog, but in the moment, I thought perhaps it was a dream sequence or Freudian psychothingy. Shortly after that, though, the fox turns up, and the rest of the opera flows naturally onward. If there are still a few mysteries to be solved along the way, they fall into the category of a director trusting the audience’s intelligence. And there are many payoffs to Kosky’s abstract interventions. Some are funny (an all-new comedy bit with an unhatched chick), some sad (the lonesome men drinking in an empty tavern), and one corrects the judgment error the composer committed by asking a teenage girl to play a rooster among hens. Instead, we get a man, Broadway and TV veteran Brian Calì, costumed with Moulin Rouge! levels of queer machismo. But no innovation is bigger than the design team’s ability to create sets of impressionistic visual splendor. Depictions of snowfall are breathtakingly beautiful, and after one moment of violence blood seems to drip from the rafters. The effects are simply dazzling. Indeed, some sets contain hidden surprises so fun that they should come with spoiler alerts. I won’t spoil those reveals. I wouldn’t dare tell you how Kosky stages the fox getting into the henhouse, the biggest laugh I’ve ever had at the opera. I won’t say how the production employs 10 acrobats, except that they’re doing something they never do at the circus. And if you don’t know what happiness comes to the fox, you’ll only be more delighted. Unusually, all the twists in The Cunning Little Vixen are in the opera’s beginning and middle stages. The ending, however, follows an inevitable logic from the moment a poacher arrives in the forest. We know the gun will go off and we'll see an allegory about life, loss, and the love-hate relationship between predator and prey. Then, suddenly, I knew what had to happen at the very end, in the final seconds. It did happen, and it didn’t surprise me except for one thing: it made me cry.
